data.title: Anthropic’s $518 billion AI infrastructure plan spans major cloud providers
data.description:
Anthropic expects to spend at least $518 billion on AI infrastructure over roughly a decade, according to a confidential IPO prospectus reviewed by Reuters.

The commitments cover cloud computing, specialised AI hardware, and infrastructure agreements with companies including Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and Broadcom. Reuters reported that around 80% of the commitments are non-cancellable or require payment regardless of usage.

According to Reuters, Anthropic’s commitments include $111.1 billion with Google, $110 billion with Amazon, and $31.4 billion with Microsoft. The filing also lists about $161.2 billion in largely non-cancellable equipment lease obligations involving Broadcom. Reuters separately reported that Anthropic spent more than $7 billion on compute and infrastructure in 2025, while its operating loss exceeded $8 billion.

Anthropic secures gigawatts of compute capacity

Amazon remains Anthropic’s primary cloud provider and training partner. The companies expanded their agreement in April this year, with Anthropic committing more than $100 billion over 10 years to AWS technologies and securing up to 5GW of additional computing capacity. Anthropic said nearly 1GW of additional Trainium2 and Trainium3 capacity would be available by the end of 2026.

Anthropic said it was already using more than one million Trainium2 chips to train and serve Claude when the agreement was announced. AWS and Anthropic also developed Project Rainier, a Trainium-based compute cluster that Anthropic uses to train and run its models. The expanded AWS agreement covers current and future generations of Trainium processors.

In October 2025, Anthropic said it planned to expand its use of Google Cloud technologies to as many as one million TPUs. The agreement was worth tens of billions of dollars and was expected to provide well over 1GW of capacity during 2026. In April this year, Anthropic expanded that relationship through an agreement with Google and Broadcom for next-generation TPU capacity expected to begin coming online in 2027. Anthropic later described that agreement as covering 5GW of capacity.

Under a separate agreement announced in November 2025, Anthropic committed to purchase $30 billion of Azure compute capacity. It also agreed to contract up to 1GW of additional capacity using Nvidia Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin systems.

Building that capacity requires expenditure before customers begin using it. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said AWS typically spends on land, power, buildings, chips, servers, and networking equipment six to 24 months before it can begin billing customers for the resulting capacity.

The agreements also give Anthropic access to different processor architectures. The company uses AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, and Nvidia GPUs for training and inference workloads. Anthropic says this allows it to match workloads with the hardware best suited to them.

Amazon said its custom chip business, including Trainium, Graviton, and Nitro, exceeded a $20 billion annual revenue run rate in early 2026. Jassy said Amazon expects Trainium, at scale, to reduce annual capital expenditure by tens of billions of dollars and provide an operating margin advantage of several percentage points compared with relying on third-party chips for inference.

Anthropic also works with AWS subsidiary Annapurna Labs on optimising future generations of Trainium for Claude workloads. Its separate partnership with Nvidia includes joint design and engineering work to optimise Anthropic models for Nvidia hardware and future Nvidia architectures for Anthropic workloads.

Cloud suppliers invest in Anthropic

Amazon has invested billions of dollars in Anthropic alongside its role as the company’s primary cloud provider and training partner. Under the partnership announced in November 2025, Nvidia committed to invest up to $10 billion in Anthropic and Microsoft up to $5 billion, alongside Anthropic’s $30 billion Azure compute commitment.

The cloud providers also distribute Claude to enterprise customers through Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, and Microsoft Foundry. Reuters reported that 47% of Anthropic’s 2025 sales passed through Amazon and Google’s cloud platforms. Anthropic identified its dependence on large technology partners as a business risk in its confidential filing.

Microsoft’s financial disclosures also show the cost of expanding AI infrastructure. Microsoft reported $59.3 billion in Microsoft Cloud revenue in its fiscal fourth quarter of 2026, up 27% year over year. Commercial remaining performance obligations – revenue contracted but not yet recognised – reached $678 billion.

The company said Microsoft Cloud gross margin percentage fell year over year partly because of continued investment in AI infrastructure and increased product usage. Nearly 90% of full-year Microsoft Cloud revenue came from customers outside frontier model companies.

Anthropic’s own revenue grew alongside its infrastructure commitments. The company reported an annualised revenue run rate of more than $30 billion in April this year, up from around $9 billion at the end of 2025. More than 1,000 business customers were each spending more than $1 million on an annualised basis at the time. The company subsequently said its annualised revenue run rate crossed $47 billion in May.

Anthropic cited capacity constraints when announcing its expanded AWS agreement in April. It said rapid consumer growth had affected reliability and performance for free, Pro, Max, and Team users, particularly during peak hours. Anthropic said additional AWS capacity would begin arriving within months.

Anthropic has also sought capacity outside the three largest cloud providers. In May this year, it announced an agreement with SpaceX giving it access to all compute capacity at the Colossus 1 data centre, with more than 300MW of capacity and over 220,000 Nvidia GPUs expected to become available that month.

(Photo by Brecht Corbeel)

data.title: Google Cloud Modernize targets AWS EKS migrations to GKE
data.description:
Google Cloud has introduced Google Cloud Modernize, bringing several of its existing migration and application modernisation services together with new AI-assisted tools aimed at infrastructure and workload migrations.

The portfolio includes Migration Center, Google Cloud VMware Engine, Google Cloud Mainframe Modernization, a new Modernization Hub, and an EKS-to-GKE migration agent. Google announced the portfolio on October 5.

Modernization Hub provides an interface within the Google Cloud console for analysing source code and mapping application dependencies. It supports modernisation work involving Java, .NET, and mainframe applications.

The hub also incorporates Google’s App Modernization CLI, or CodMod, which uses Gemini models to analyse source code repositories, identify dependencies, and generate modernisation recommendations. Google said the tooling can be used when moving older .NET Framework applications to .NET running in Linux containers.

Google targets EKS workloads with migration agent

One of the new components is Google’s EKS-to-GKE Agentic Migration tool, which is currently in public preview. It is designed to assist organisations moving Kubernetes workloads from Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service to Google Kubernetes Engine.

The migration agent handles some of the cloud-specific configuration changes involved in moving Kubernetes workloads between AWS and Google Cloud. Google said it can translate AWS IAM Roles for Service Accounts to Google Cloud Workload Identity, map Application Load Balancer ingress configurations to the Kubernetes Gateway API, and convert Karpenter node configurations for use with GKE’s node provisioning tools.

The tool can scan an EKS cluster or source repository, identify application dependencies and AWS-specific configurations, and generate Terraform modules for the target Google Cloud environment. It also handles Kubernetes manifest translation and mappings for storage and networking between the two platforms.

Google said the migration process covers discovery, planning, infrastructure generation, application translation, and validation. Generated infrastructure is checked using tools including Terraform validation and Kubernetes manifest validation before it is submitted for review.

The agent does not apply generated configurations directly to a live GKE cluster. Instead, it creates pull requests that can pass through existing CI/CD and approval workflows before deployment.

The tool also does not move stateful application data. Google said it generates migration runbooks that can direct teams to services such as Database Migration Service or Storage Transfer Service.

Application testing, architecture decisions, data migration, and the final production cutover remain outside the agent’s scope, according to analysts cited by Network World.

The EKS tool builds on existing AWS discovery support in Google Cloud Migration Center. Google has added support for assessing AWS resources including EC2-related infrastructure, Elastic Block Store, AWS Application Load Balancer, Elastic Container Registry, DynamoDB, API Gateway, Glue, Kinesis, and ElastiCache.

The wider Modernize portfolio also covers VMware infrastructure, Java and .NET applications, mainframes, and other workloads being assessed for migration to Google Cloud.

Google broadens migration and modernisation tooling

Google has also added Gemini-based capabilities to Migration Center’s Quick TCO Estimator.

Organisations can upload VMware inventory data or enter infrastructure details manually to model how workloads would run on Compute Engine. The calculations can include CPU and memory utilisation, storage, deployment region, software licensing, support costs, discounts, and estimated migration costs.

Google Cloud documentation says the tool can produce one-year and five-year total cost of ownership comparisons. Users can also adjust assumptions through a Gemini-powered interface, including deployment configuration and licensing inputs for Windows Server and SQL Server.

Beyond Kubernetes, Modernization Hub can also analyse Java and .NET application estates.

Google’s application modernisation tooling can analyse Java and .NET repositories, map dependencies, and identify components that need to change before applications are moved to newer runtimes or container environments.

Pareekh Jain, principal analyst at Pareekh Consulting, said organisations running combinations of VMware, Java, mainframe, Oracle, and Kubernetes workloads have traditionally needed separate assessment tools and migration teams, according to Network World. Google has brought several of those functions together under Modernize.

Mainframe workloads are covered through Google’s Mainframe Assessment Tool, Mainframe Connector, and Dual Run. The assessment tool analyses source code and dependencies, while Mainframe Connector can move and convert data stored in mainframe formats such as EBCDIC for use with Google Cloud services.

Dual Run allows organisations to operate workloads on an existing mainframe and Google Cloud in parallel and compare their outputs before production cutover.

The portfolio also includes infrastructure options for workloads moved to Google Cloud. The M4N Series provides 26.57 GiB of memory per virtual CPU and supports Hyperdisk Extreme. Google said M4N’s memory-to-core ratio can reduce software licensing costs by more than 20% for Oracle and other core-licensed databases by reducing the number of processor cores required.

VMware environments are supported through Google’s self-managed VMware offering on Bare Metal Z3 instances running VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1. Those environments can connect to services including Compute Engine, GKE, and BigQuery through Google Cloud’s virtual private cloud network.

(Photo by Ameer Basheer)

data.title: Microsoft to invest $10 billion in Gulf cloud and AI infrastructure
data.description:
Microsoft plans to invest more than $10 billion across Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates through 2030, with spending directed towards cloud and AI infrastructure and its operations in the region.

The investment will include capital and operating expenditure as Microsoft expands computing capacity across the four Gulf states. The company has not provided a country-by-country or project-level breakdown of the spending, citing security considerations.

Microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith told Reuters that the spending covers both infrastructure construction and the expansion of the company’s regional operations.

“We’re sustaining all the investments we planned to make before this conflict started, and we’re in fact adding to them,” Smith said.

Other hyperscalers are also committing capital to cloud and AI infrastructure in Gulf markets. AWS has committed more than $5.3 billion to infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, while Oracle announced a $14 billion investment in the Kingdom over 10 years covering cloud and AI technology.

Google already operates its Dammam cloud region in Saudi Arabia and has partnered with the country’s Public Investment Fund on an AI hub linked to its existing regional infrastructure.

Cloud competition moves deeper into infrastructure

Microsoft also plans to spend more than $400 million on subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030. The investment will build on infrastructure that includes the SeaMeWe-6 subsea cable system, which has landing points in Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE.

Microsoft’s planned spending covers both cloud and AI capacity and the subsea and terrestrial network infrastructure supporting regional connectivity.

Submarine cables carry more than 99% of international data traffic, according to the International Telecommunication Union. The ITU says disruptions caused by human activity and natural hazards can affect government and industry operations, while geographic concentration and dependence on a small number of cable systems can create additional resilience risks.

The ITU’s 2026 submarine cable resilience work also identified long repair times and limited geographic diversity as risks to international connectivity. It recommended measures including faster repair processes and greater diversity in cable routes.

Microsoft said the broader investment will support long-term cloud and AI capacity commitments across the four countries. The plans were outlined during a roundtable held alongside the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

The company is also expanding relationships with regional governments and AI organisations. These include G42 in the UAE, HUMAIN in Saudi Arabia, QAI in Qatar, and the Government of Kuwait.

Microsoft invested $1.5 billion for a minority stake in Abu Dhabi-based G42 in 2024. Smith told Reuters that Microsoft is working with HUMAIN and QAI in selected areas but does not plan to make capital investments in the two companies.

Microsoft and G42 have also committed to expanding data centre capacity in the UAE. In November 2025, the companies announced a 200MW expansion through G42 subsidiary Khazna Data Centers, with capacity expected to begin coming online before the end of 2026.

Microsoft’s Saudi Arabia East cloud region is another part of its regional infrastructure expansion. The company confirmed in August that the region will become available to customers in November 2026.

Located in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province, the region will comprise three Azure Availability Zones, providing separate infrastructure locations within the same region.

AWS is pursuing a similar regional architecture in Saudi Arabia. Its Saudi infrastructure region, backed by more than $5.3 billion in planned investment, is also designed with three Availability Zones.

AWS already operates a three-zone region in the UAE, where it outlined $5 billion in planned investment through 2036 for the construction and operation of the region.

Sovereignty and resilience shape Gulf cloud build-out

Microsoft is also adding a Middle East Digital Resilience initiative to its regional plans. It will provide organisations with resilience assessments, reference architectures, readiness guidance, and programmes focused on continuity and recovery.

Reuters reported that Microsoft has already provided digital resilience assessments to local partners following regional disruption. The company is also working with Gulf countries on readiness and the protection of critical data.

Microsoft plans to extend its data protection, sovereignty, and business continuity commitments to eligible governments and customers in the region. The services will include Microsoft Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud, and Project Digital Shield.

The sovereign cloud component sits alongside existing cloud and cybersecurity requirements in Gulf markets. Saudi Arabia maintains dedicated rules for cloud service providers and separate cybersecurity controls covering providers and cloud customers.

Saudi Arabia’s National Cybersecurity Authority published its updated Cloud Cybersecurity Controls in July 2025, reflecting changes related to data localisation requirements. The controls set minimum cybersecurity requirements for cloud service providers and tenants operating in the country.

Saudi Arabia also operates a Cloud First Policy, developed in 2018 and updated in 2020, aimed at encouraging cloud adoption across government and private-sector organisations.

The UAE’s National Cloud Security Policy covers areas including data security, sovereignty, infrastructure, and cloud service providers, while Qatar’s Cloud Policy Framework addresses security, privacy, data protection, and regulatory requirements for its cloud ecosystem.

Google’s Dammam region shows how cloud providers are structuring operations around local market requirements. Saudi customers accessing the region purchase Google Cloud services through CNTXT, Google’s exclusive reseller for the region.

Microsoft will also expand cooperation with national cybersecurity authorities in Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE. The company said dedicated cybersecurity personnel will support work in each country.

The Saudi Arabia East region is scheduled to become available in November later this year, while Microsoft’s wider infrastructure, connectivity, cybersecurity, and sovereign cloud programmes are planned to continue through 2030.

(Photo by Anna Surovková)

data.title: AWS and Azure face EU gatekeeper rules over cloud lock-in
data.description:
Microsoft Azure and AWS are moving closer to being designated as gatekeepers under the European Union’s Digital Markets Act, which would bring the two cloud platforms under additional competition rules.

The European Commission is preparing to conclude its investigations into Azure and AWS, with draft findings that the two services meet the requirements for designation, Bloomberg reported on October 2, citing people familiar with the matter. A decision is expected in November, although the findings remain in draft form and the timing could change.

The Commission said no final decision has been taken. It sent preliminary findings to Amazon and Microsoft in June as part of investigations into whether their cloud businesses should fall within the scope of the DMA.

EU scrutiny focuses on cloud lock-in

The Commission said in June that AWS and Azure should be designated as gatekeepers, despite neither service meeting the DMA’s standard quantitative thresholds.

AWS and Azure are the largest and second-largest cloud computing services in the EU, respectively, according to the Commission. Regulators concluded that both act as important gateways between businesses and their customers in the region.

The Commission is assessing both services through the DMA’s qualitative designation process. The regulation allows services that fall below its standard numerical thresholds to be designated if a market investigation finds they have a substantial impact on the EU market, act as an important gateway between businesses and end users, and hold an entrenched and durable position.

The investigations began in November 2025, when the Commission opened proceedings to determine whether AWS and Azure should be designated despite falling below the standard thresholds.

The Commission cited the companies’ established user bases, wider technology ecosystems, high switching costs, and customer lock-in as factors in its preliminary assessment.

Regulators also pointed to the role of AI in cloud procurement. The Commission said the AI tools and partnerships offered by Amazon and Microsoft have become a factor in customers’ choice of cloud provider.

Amazon and Microsoft have already been designated as gatekeepers under the DMA for other services.

Switching and interoperability face closer attention

If AWS and Azure are designated, Amazon and Microsoft would have six months to bring the cloud services into compliance with applicable DMA obligations.

The Commission is separately examining whether the DMA’s existing rules are sufficient for cloud computing. That investigation covers interoperability barriers, restrictions on business users’ access to data, tying and bundling, financial conditions, and contractual terms between providers and customers.

A Commission stakeholder roundtable in July examined related issues, including technical interoperability, financial conditions, and commercial practices affecting cloud switching.

Cloud switching is already covered by the EU Data Act, which requires providers of data-processing services to remove commercial, technical, contractual, and organisational obstacles that prevent customers from moving to another provider or using several services at the same time.

The Commission identifies barriers including data-egress charges, lengthy switching procedures, and a lack of interoperability between providers.

For infrastructure services, providers must take reasonable measures to help customers achieve functionally equivalent outcomes after moving to another service of the same type. Providers are also required to supply relevant documentation, technical support, and switching capabilities where applicable.

Other data-processing services must provide open interfaces to support data portability and interoperability between providers.

The Data Act is also phasing out charges associated with cloud switching. From January 12, 2027, providers will no longer be permitted to impose switching charges, including data-egress charges that arise as part of the switching process. Until then, reduced switching charges cannot exceed the costs directly linked to the move.

The Commission’s broader DMA cloud investigation also examines access to business-user data, bundling practices, financial conditions, and contractual arrangements. The separate investigation is due to conclude with a final report by May 2027.

The Commission has not yet set out how every DMA obligation would apply to the two cloud platforms.

AWS and Microsoft push back on findings

Amazon has opposed the Commission’s preliminary assessment. The company previously said the findings do not reflect the range of cloud services available to European customers and warned that additional regulation could affect investment and innovation.

Microsoft has raised concerns about the treatment of Google Cloud. The company said in June that excluding Google’s cloud and AI businesses from comparable scrutiny risked creating an uneven market.

The Commission has maintained that the investigations remain ongoing and that both companies have an opportunity to respond before it reaches a final decision.

The Data Act and DMA impose different requirements on the cloud market. The Data Act sets rules for switching and interoperability across data-processing services, while the DMA imposes conduct obligations on companies and services designated as gatekeepers.

The Commission has described cloud services as a cornerstone of Europe’s economy and a prerequisite for AI. More than half of EU businesses used paid cloud computing services in 2025, according to Eurostat.

A final designation would bring AWS and Azure directly within the DMA framework for their cloud computing services. The Commission has not publicly confirmed the November timetable reported by Bloomberg.

(Photo by Antoine Schibler)

data.title: Best Auth0 Alternatives for AI Agent Authentication and Authorisation in 2026
data.description:
AI agents aren’t a future curiosity; they’re pouring into production at breakneck speed, and most of your IAM stack wasn’t built for them. Designed around human login flows, classic platforms like Auth0 fall short when every agent needs its own identity, machine-speed tokens, and permissions that don’t simply inherit a user’s full access. 

The numbers paint a stark picture. A 2025 EMA report, compiled for Ory,  found that 79% of organisations lack written policies for governing AI agents, yet those agents are already deployed in production environments. 

Meanwhile, Palo Alto Networks’ 2026 Identity Security Landscape report notes that machine identities, including AI agents, now outnumber human identities by a staggering 109:1, and Help Net Security’s coverage of the same report projects an 85% growth in AI agents over the next 12 months, with machine identities set to increase by 77%.

And the broader IAM foundation is already wobbling. A Cloud Computing News investigation showed that cloud misconfiguration and identity access management risks are rampant, with 97.1% of organisations using privileged user access controls without Multi‑Factor Authentication (MFA) enforcement in cloud environments. 

Adding to the visibility nightmare, enterprises struggle with identity visibility across cloud apps, a problem that becomes catastrophic when autonomous agents are roaming those same environments. 

Agent identities demand API‑first authentication, fine‑grained scoping, delegation chains, native MCP protocol support, and immutable audit trails. They don’t just log in; they negotiate, delegate, and act on your behalf. 

If your identity stack treats every service account as a human user with a permanent password, you’re carrying technical debt that’s about to compound.

What does a modern alternative look like? An API‑first platform that can spin up machine principals as easily as human ones, issue short‑lived tokens, understand tool‑level permissions, and trace every action back through a delegation chain that outlives the token itself. 

That’s the benchmark for this list.

Methodology & Evaluation Criteria

We evaluated these platforms for cloud teams moving from Auth0 to a solution designed for autonomous agents at machine scale, not just human logins. The ranking rests on five criteria:

  1. API‑first design — headless, OAuth 2.1/OIDC certified, built for machine clients.
  2. Fine‑grained authorisation — RBAC + ReBAC, tool‑level scoping, and agent‑specific policies that avoid blanket permission inheritance.
  3. MCP (Model Context Protocol) support — native OAuth 2.1 authorisation server for MCP, Dynamic Client Registration (DCR), PKCE, and token introspection.
  4. Audit trail depth — immutable delegation chains, SIEM streaming, and correlation IDs that span agent actions from initiation to final API call.
  5. Scalability & cost predictability — horizontal scale, sub‑10ms latency, and transparent pricing without per‑agent billing surprises.

A secondary filter considered developer experience: SDKs for code‑agent integrations, drag‑and‑drop tooling, and the quality of open‑source documentation. 

The ranking is editorial, built on these criteria, with Ory, thanks to its open‑source Zanzibar authorisation engine, certified OAuth2 infrastructure, and a dedicated agent security stack.

1. Ory – Modular, API-First, Zanzibar-Powered Agent Identity

Ory is a modular, multi‑deployment IAM platform that serves humans, B2B workloads, and AI agents from a unified composable stack. At its core sits Ory Hydra, an OpenID Foundation‑certified OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect server that securely anchors OpenAI’s 1.2 billion weekly active users. 

Alongside Ory Hydra, Ory Keto brings a Zanzibar‑based authorisation engine for both RBAC and relationship‑based access control (ReBAC), while a separate Agent Security/DX layer adds everything agents need: dedicated identities, tool‑level scoping, and native MCP integration. 

The entire platform runs identically whether you deploy across self-managed environments (on-premises or private cloud) with an Ory Enterprise License, or choose a fully managed SaaS platform via Ory Network. 

  • API-first & scalable: Ory Hydra is stateless and horizontally scalable, engineered to deliver the low-latency token validation that demanding machine workloads require. Built for massive enterprise throughput, Ory’s architecture actively anchors over 3.25 billion global identities and handles 4.4 billion daily transactions, with an enterprise footprint that has surpassed 700+ million Docker image pulls.
  • Fine‑grained authorisation: Ory Keto delivers distributed Zanzibar‑grade authorisation with sub‑10ms P95 latency and >99.99% availability. A single permissions API models both RBAC and ReBAC, so you can scope an agent to exactly the commands, MCP tools, and API endpoints it needs, without accidentally leaking broader user privileges.
  • MCP support & agent security: The Ory agent security platform handles OAuth 2.1 with PKCE, Dynamic Client Registration, and token introspection. Every agent and sub‑agent gets its own credential; every shell command, file write, and tool invocation goes through Ory Keto’s engine to enforce strict policy rules at the exact moment an AI agent performs an action. The  full delegation chain is recorded in OpenTelemetry and streamed to your SIEM.
  • Agent DX: Announced in June 2026, Ory Agent DX plugs identity management directly into coding agents like Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Gemini CLI, among many others. Developers can scaffold OAuth‑based auth workflows in natural language from inside their IDE, dramatically shortening the path from prototype to production.

Best for technical teams that require highly engineered, modular, structural control, total deployment flexibility across self-managed or cloud environments, Zanzibar‑grade authorisation built to handle machine-scale transaction volumes. For those searching for robust Ory AI agent authentication with complete delegation chains and tool‑level policy control, Ory’s composable engine is purpose‑made. 

Less ideal if your team insists on a fully no‑code platform with zero operational overhead, though the fully managed SaaS option via Ory Network significantly narrows that gap by removing infrastructure maintenance.  

User signals, including discussions on r/webdev, note a learning curve when modeling intricate ReBAC relationships, but the platform’s modularity rewards the investment.

2. WorkOS – Enterprise Auth with Fine-Grained Authorisation (FGA) for Agents

WorkOS is known for enterprise SSO and directory sync, but in February 2026 it launched Fine-Grained Authorisation (FGA) specifically to close the authorisation gap for AI agents. Its AuthKit functions as an OAuth 2.1 authorisation server that works with the official MCP SDKs, and the platform bundles SSO, SCIM provisioning, and detailed audit logs. 

WorkOS also aligns with emerging standards, the IETF’s proposed /Agents SCIM resource type, currently an Internet-Draft with no formal standing in the IETF standards process, and NIST’s early‑2026 agent identity paper. It positions itself as an independent enterprise auth layer for B2B SaaS companies that are now dealing with agent‑heavy architectures.

  • Agent‑specific FGA: Tool‑level permission scoping and an intersection‑rule check prevent agents from inheriting broader user entitlements. An agent can only access what it’s explicitly granted, even if the human behind it holds wider permissions.
  • MCP & standards alignment: The 2026 AI agent auth checklist outlines how AuthKit handles OAuth 2.1 for MCP servers, SCIM for agent user lifecycle, and audit trails that tie into enterprise compliance workflows. Early alignment with IETF and NIST drafts signals that WorkOS is watching governance deadlines as closely as engineering needs.
  • Enterprise‑grade feature set: In addition to FGA, the platform includes directory sync, inbound SSO, an admin portal, and machine‑to‑machine credentials, all shipped as a single API.

Best for B2B SaaS teams already in the WorkOS ecosystem that want SSO, FGA, and MCP compatibility in one enterprise package. 

Less ideal if you require deep self‑hosting control or a lean budget. 

Community feedback from r/nextjs highlights frustration with a $100/month custom domain fee and occasional friction accessing user‑org data client‑side, which may be deal‑breakers for smaller teams.

3. Stytch (a Twilio company) – Intelligent Agent Detection and OAuth 2.1 MCP Auth

Twilio acquired Stytch in November 2025, cementing it as the intelligent identity layer for AI agents and humans. Stytch’s Connected Apps platform implements OAuth 2.1 with PKCE and Dynamic Client Registration, plus a consent UI that can drop onto your existing CIAM provider without a full user‑database migration. 

The standout differentiator is agent awareness: Stytch can detect AI agents on arrival and route them to the right MCP endpoints while blocking bad bots.

  • Agent detection & routing: Stytch’s ‘isAgent’ capability identifies autonomous agents as they arrive and directs them to the appropriate OAuth flow, with built‑in bot detection that squashes malicious actors before they can probe your endpoints.
  • OAuth 2.1 MCP layer: An AI agent authentication guide details how Connected Apps works as a standalone OAuth 2.1 layer above your current CIAM, so you can add agent‑specific auth without tearing out your existing login system.
  • Twilio backing: The acquisition provides enterprise stability and a clearer long‑term roadmap, which matters when you’re betting on a relatively young identity vendor.
  • Multi‑tenancy support: RBAC, SCIM, and SSO are built in for B2B scenarios, so you don’t have to swap platforms as your customer base grows.

Best for teams that want an agent‑detection overlay they can place on top of their current CIAM without a migration, and value the safety net of a major parent company. 

Less ideal if you require granular policy orchestration for complex multi-tenant B2B hierarchies or the flexibility to deploy outside a vendor-managed SaaS model into self-managed environments.

Third‑party validation is thin: Trustpilot shows zero reviews, and a lone 28‑view YouTube review doesn’t substitute for peer benchmarking. Plan to validate the agent detection in your own sandbox.

4. Descope – No-Code Agentic Identity Hub with Pre-Built MCP Templates

Descope’s Agentic Identity Hub 2.0, launched in January 2026, takes a no‑code/low‑code approach to AI agent lifecycle management. It provisions dedicated agent identities, provides an MCP authentication module (OAuth 2.1 + PKCE + DCR + CIMD), includes a credential vault with 50+ prebuilt connection templates, and layers on enterprise policy controls with SIEM‑streaming audit logs. 

Used by 1,000+ organisations, Descope offers a no-code/low-code customer and agentic identity platform., including GoFundMe, Databricks, and GoodRx.

  • Hub 2.0 capabilities: A turnkey MCP auth suite, a vault that accelerates integrations with common APIs, and enterprise‑grade policies with audit logging that feeds directly into Splunk, Datadog, or your SIEM of choice.
  • Market readiness insight: Descope’s own survey of 400+ identity decision‑makers found that only 37% had moved past pilot stages, and 2,000 MCP servers were found to have no authentication at all. This is a vivid reminder that the market is wide open but urgently needs help.
  • Rapid adoption: Over 1,000 organisations are already onboard, including recognisable names like You.com and Navan, which indicates the no‑code model is landing with teams that lack deep identity engineering benches.
  • Developer experience: A drag‑and‑drop workflow designer and a modest but active YouTube channel make onboarding approachable, though the audience remains practitioner‑sized (1.3K subscribers, 179 videos, with low view counts on recent videos).

Best for teams that want to move fast with pre‑built templates and no‑code flows, especially if you don’t employ dedicated identity engineers. 

Less ideal if you require full customisation control or the ability to host infrastructure in self-managed environments. 

The no‑code abstraction can feel limiting when you need to model unique agent‑authorisation graphs that don’t fit the preset templates.

5. Keycloak – Self-Hosted Alternative for DIY Agent Auth

Keycloak, maintained by Red Hat, is a mature open‑source IAM solution that can be configured for machine‑to‑machine OAuth 2.0 client‑credentials flows, a basic scaffolding for AI agent authentication. 

Keycloak supports MCP as an authorisation server, complying with OAuth 2.0 standards and providing fine-grained authorisation services. It appeals primarily to organisations already invested in self-managed IAM and comfortable writing the missing pieces.

  • DIY adaptability: Admins can create machine‑to‑machine clients and define fine‑grained roles, but every agent‑specific capability, like delegation, bot detection, MCP auth, must be built in‑house.
  • Self‑hosting preference: The 2025 EMA report shows that 72.1% of organisations prefer self‑managed LLM deployment, and that preference correlates with self‑managed IAM. But Keycloak’s agent‑native gap undercuts that advantage.
  • Resource‑intensive: Expect to invest significant DevOps and identity‑engineering hours for ongoing maintenance and the inevitable agent‑specific extensions.

Best for organisations with large‑scale Keycloak deployments and the engineering capacity to extend it for agent identities. 

Less ideal if you want a turnkey, agent‑specific solution with MCP support and immutable delegation trails out of the box. 

Factor in the total cost of building, and forever maintaining, those missing pieces before assuming open source is cheaper.

Caveats & Counterpoints

The agent identity space is still forming. The EMA report, cited earlier, found that most organisations are unprepared across all four IAM readiness dimensions for AI agents: 61.6% on Security, 62.0% on Scale, 48.7% on Compliance, and 59.4% on Resiliency. 

The EMA report further highlights that while 60.5% of organisations use a hybrid human/service-account management model for agents, only 23.6% treat them purely as service accounts, and 10% manage them as human identities, meaning many aren’t organisationally ready to adopt dedicated agent identities yet. 

Furthermore, IAM cost anxiety adds another layer: the same report reveals that 47% of organisations already worry about rising or unpredictable costs with their current providers, and 41% report security or reliability concerns.

Buyer maturity must be weighed against each platform’s trade‑offs. Ory’s composable flexibility carries a learning curve for complex ReBAC models. WorkOS’s enterprise feature set comes with a premium monthly fee and less self‑hosting freedom. Stytch’s agent‑detection narrative is still light on independent validation. Descope’s no‑code abstraction may chafe teams that need to model non‑standard authorisation relationships. Keycloak, while free, shifts the development burden onto your engineers. 

MCP adoption is accelerating. The protocol was donated to the Linux Foundation’s Agentic AI Foundation in late 2025, and all the listed platforms (except Keycloak) are iterating quickly.

Evaluate roadmaps, not just today’s feature snapshots.

Conclusion

Every alternative here can do what Auth0 was never designed to do: treat AI agents as first‑class principals, not as human‑user shadows. The right fit depends on your starting point.

data.title: AWS to disconnect European Sovereign Cloud from global network in independence test
data.description:
AWS plans to temporarily disconnect its European Sovereign Cloud from the company’s global network backbone on October 24, in an exercise designed to demonstrate that the environment can operate without infrastructure outside the European Union.

The exercise will run for several hours, during which the AWS European Sovereign Cloud will operate without a connection to the AWS Global Network. AWS said service availability within the sovereign cloud, other AWS Regions, and private connectivity through AWS Direct Connect will not be affected.

Customers could experience brief connectivity disruptions when traffic is moved to an alternative network route at the start and end of the test. AWS said these disruptions could occur while external networks update their routing information.

AWS tests operations without its global backbone

The AWS Global Network is the company’s private backbone for moving authorised operational data between AWS locations without using the public internet. Under normal operations, the European Sovereign Cloud uses this network for connectivity.

The exercise will not disconnect the European Sovereign Cloud from the internet. AWS will instead use dedicated internet connectivity supplied by European internet service providers, allowing workloads to remain reachable while the company’s private global backbone is unavailable.

AWS said traffic that would normally move across its private backbone will be rerouted over the public internet for the duration of the exercise. The company expects brief periods of routing convergence when traffic switches to the European ISP connections and again when it returns to the AWS Global Network.

AWS also uses a separate global system for limited transfers of operational data associated with the European Sovereign Cloud. The company said its EU-based team controls these transfers and that customer content and customer-created metadata are not included.

According to AWS, the system is also used for vetted source-code mirroring and software updates, while transferring a limited amount of approved operational information outside the EU. The company plans to disable the system entirely during the October exercise.

The Global Network backbone and operational-data transfer system are the two links to AWS’s wider global infrastructure that will be removed during the test. AWS said neither is critical to operating the European Sovereign Cloud, with the exercise intended to provide technical evidence for that claim.

The test will be conducted by the European Sovereign Cloud operations team, which AWS said consists entirely of EU residents working within the EU. The team will use hardware and software resources available within the sovereign cloud during the exercise.

AWS said it plans to share an update with customers and regulators after the test.

Data residency is only one layer of cloud sovereignty

Keeping data within the EU is only one part of the European Commission’s approach to cloud sovereignty. Its Cloud Sovereignty Framework assesses providers across eight categories, including legal and jurisdictional sovereignty, data and AI sovereignty, operational sovereignty, supply chains, technology, security and compliance, and strategic considerations.

The framework separates data location from operational control. Data sovereignty covers issues such as where data is stored and processed, while operational sovereignty includes whether EU-based operators can manage, maintain, and support a service without requiring non-EU vendor involvement.

AWS said customer content and customer-created metadata in the European Sovereign Cloud remain within the EU. The October exercise instead tests whether the environment can continue operating when its normal connections to AWS’s global systems are removed.

The European Commission also treats sovereignty as a graduated requirement rather than a single designation. Its Cloud Sovereignty Framework uses Sovereignty Effectiveness Assurance Levels, or SEALs, with SEAL-2 corresponding to data sovereignty, SEAL-3 covering technological autonomy and digital resilience, and SEAL-4 representing full sovereignty.

The framework applies 48 criteria across areas including legal jurisdiction, operations, supply chains, and underlying technology. These criteria allow data residency to be assessed separately from operational and technological dependencies.

AWS made the European Sovereign Cloud generally available in January 2026, with its first Region located in Brandenburg, Germany. AWS said the infrastructure is physically and logically separate from the company’s existing commercial AWS Regions.

The separation also extends to the cloud’s control plane. AWS said the European Sovereign Cloud operates as its own AWS partition, called aws-eusc, with separate identity and access management, billing, console, service endpoints, and organisational systems.

AWS partitions create boundaries between groups of Regions. Credentials used in AWS’s standard commercial partition cannot be used to access resources in aws-eusc, and services such as cross-partition role assumption, VPC peering, Transit Gateway peering, and S3 replication are not available across the boundary.

Customers therefore operate separate AWS organisations and billing systems inside the European Sovereign Cloud. AWS documentation states that cross-partition applications must integrate through network or API connections using separate credentials rather than shared AWS account trust.

The architecture also uses separate networking infrastructure for AWS Direct Connect. AWS said Direct Connect connections or gateways used in the commercial AWS partition cannot be extended directly into the European Sovereign Cloud, requiring separate connectivity into the aws-eusc environment.

AWS said day-to-day operations, including data-centre access, technical support, and customer service, are handled by personnel based in the EU.

The company has also placed a local copy of source code within the EU. AWS said the environment has no critical operational dependencies on infrastructure outside the region, a claim the October exercise is intended to test under live operating conditions.

EU rules separate operations from provider control

Operational independence does not cover every aspect of cloud sovereignty considered by European regulators. AWS remains headquartered in the United States, while the European Commission assesses legal and jurisdictional sovereignty separately from data location and day-to-day cloud operations.

The Commission’s proposed Cloud and AI Development Act makes that distinction explicit. Its first assurance level covers data processing and storage on infrastructure located in the EU, while higher levels add requirements around independence from third countries, EU ownership and control, personnel, and software supply chains.

The proposed structure separates where workloads run from who controls the provider and its supporting technology. AWS’s October test addresses the operational layer rather than provider ownership or all of the legal and supply-chain criteria covered by the EU frameworks.

The European Commission introduced its Cloud Sovereignty Framework as part of a €180 million procurement programme for cloud services used by EU institutions, bodies, offices, and agencies.

Providers in that procurement were assessed using both SEAL thresholds and the wider 48-criterion sovereignty framework, covering legal jurisdiction, data and AI, operations, supply chains, technology, security, and compliance.

The Commission’s proposed Cloud and AI Development Act would establish a single EU-wide framework for assessing cloud and AI sovereignty. It would also introduce common procurement requirements for public administrations and measures aimed at reducing dependencies in critical digital infrastructure.

AWS said the exercise was designed to align with the objectives of the European Commission’s Cloud Sovereignty Framework and the C3A framework from Germany’s Federal Office for Information Security, or BSI. The company expects the results to provide additional technical and operational evidence for customers and regulators assessing its sovereignty controls.

data.title: Alibaba Cloud plans 20GW AI infrastructure expansion by 2032
data.description:
Alibaba Cloud plans to expand its global data centre capacity to more than 20 gigawatts by 2032 as the company increases infrastructure spending for AI computing.

Alibaba Group CEO Eddie Wu announced the target at the company’s Apsara Conference in Hangzhou yesterday. Alibaba did not disclose its current data centre capacity or provide a regional breakdown for the planned expansion.

The target follows Alibaba’s February 2025 commitment to invest more than 380 billion yuan, or about US$52 billion at the time, in cloud computing and AI infrastructure over three years. The company said the spending would exceed its investment in those areas over the previous decade.

The expansion covers more than data centre capacity. Alibaba is also developing its own AI accelerators, server processors, networking and storage systems, cloud services, and Qwen models. Wu described the strategy at Apsara as covering the full AI technology stack, including models, semiconductors, and data centres.

In the June quarter of 2026, Alibaba’s AI Cloud and Compute Services revenue reached US$7.1 billion, up 45% year over year. Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, and amortisation for the cloud segment rose 133% to US$830 million, while its adjusted EBITA margin reached about 12%. Alibaba said revenue from AI-related products recorded triple-digit growth for the twelfth consecutive quarter.

Reuters reported in August that Alibaba had already spent about half of its planned 380 billion yuan AI investment during 2026 as the company increased spending on proprietary chips and AI infrastructure. Wu also said Alibaba expected margins to improve as it deployed more processors developed by its T-Head semiconductor unit and replaced some commercially procured chips in its data centres.

Wu said at Apsara that customer demand for AI services was exceeding Alibaba Cloud’s available supply, according to Reuters. He added that supply-chain constraints were limiting how quickly the company could expand capacity and said Alibaba Cloud would begin bringing AI supernodes into commercial operation at scale during the current quarter.

Alibaba builds more of its AI infrastructure

Alibaba also introduced the Zhenwu V900, an AI processor designed by its T-Head semiconductor unit for model training and inference. The processor has 216GB of memory and 1,200GB/s of inter-chip bandwidth, with support for data formats including FP8 and FP4.

The company said the V900 delivers three times the performance of the Zhenwu M890, which Alibaba introduced in May. The V900 is scheduled to enter mass production and commercial release in the first quarter of 2027.

The V900 extends the processor roadmap Alibaba outlined with the M890 earlier this year. Reuters reported that Alibaba developed the Zhenwu line as Chinese technology companies sought domestic alternatives to Nvidia processors amid US restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China.

Alibaba’s earlier M890 launch also connected its custom processors more closely with its cloud infrastructure. The company introduced the Panjiu AL128 server system with 128 M890 accelerators in a rack and made it available to enterprise customers through Alibaba Cloud’s Bailian platform. T-Head said in May that it had shipped more than 560,000 Zhenwu processors to more than 400 external customers across 20 industries.

Alibaba is integrating the V900 into an upgraded supernode server alongside its own networking, storage, and interface components. The system is designed to support clusters containing as many as 500,000 accelerator cards, according to the company.

Alibaba’s chip roadmap also covers general-purpose processors. The company plans to introduce its Yitian 720 and Yitian 730 CPUs in 2027, with the latter based on T-Head’s own microarchitecture.

Alibaba has already deployed T-Head processors within its cloud infrastructure. In a May shareholder letter, the company said its proprietary AI chips had entered production at scale and were supplying computing capacity to Alibaba Cloud infrastructure and its model-as-a-service inference platform.

Alibaba Cloud also announced updates to the networking and storage systems used by large AI clusters. Its HPN 8.0 Pro networking architecture provides 100 petabits of bandwidth and supports more than 130,000 network ports operating at 800Gbps within a single cluster, according to Alibaba.

Its Cloud Parallel File Storage system is designed for AI training workloads and supports throughput measured in hundreds of terabytes per second, as well as hundreds of millions of input/output operations per second. Alibaba said the system can reduce AI storage costs by 69%, although the company did not provide independent benchmark data alongside the announcement.

As accelerator clusters grow, networking bandwidth and storage throughput become more important to keeping compute resources utilised. Google has identified similar constraints in its own AI infrastructure, particularly as larger clusters place greater demands on networks and storage systems.

Google’s AI Hypercomputer architecture combines processors, networking, storage, and orchestration software. Its infrastructure includes Google TPUs and Axion CPUs alongside Nvidia GPUs and Intel and AMD processors, as well as its Virgo data centre network and high-performance storage systems.

Hyperscalers develop more custom infrastructure

AWS, Microsoft, and Google have also developed custom processors while continuing to use hardware from outside suppliers. AWS operates Trainium AI processors and Graviton CPUs, Microsoft uses Maia accelerators and Cobalt CPUs across Azure, while Google combines its TPUs and Axion CPUs with Nvidia, Intel, and AMD hardware.

Amazon has cited price-performance and infrastructure economics as reasons for developing its own processors. The company said Trainium2 offered about 30% better price-performance than comparable GPUs, while Trainium3 improved price-performance by another 30% to 40% over Trainium2. Those figures are based on Amazon’s own measurements.

AWS also uses custom silicon for general-purpose cloud workloads. Amazon introduced Graviton in 2018 and said in April 2026 that more than 90,000 customers were using Graviton-based infrastructure.

Microsoft said in its fiscal 2026 third-quarter earnings call that millions of servers across its fleet use Microsoft-designed networking, security, and virtualisation silicon. Its Maia 200 AI accelerator was operating in data centres in Iowa and Arizona, while Cobalt CPUs had been deployed in nearly half of Microsoft’s data centre regions.

All three providers continue to use third-party hardware alongside their own silicon. Microsoft deploys its processors alongside Nvidia and AMD hardware, Google supports TPUs alongside Nvidia GPUs, and AWS has said it will continue offering Nvidia systems as it expands Trainium.

Alibaba connects infrastructure to cloud services

The hardware sits underneath Alibaba’s cloud services for deploying and operating AI applications. Its AgentCore platform is designed to manage agents through development and deployment, while Agent Security Center provides security and compliance controls for agent-based applications.

Alibaba said in a May shareholder letter that the growth focus of its cloud business was moving from traditional compute and storage toward models, AI computing, and agent services.

Alibaba’s infrastructure plans also extend to larger Qwen models. Qwen 4 is currently in training, while future Qwen 4.5 and Qwen 5 models are planned with between five trillion and 10 trillion parameters, compared with 2.4 trillion parameters for the current Qwen 3.8 Max model.

data.title: IBM VMware cloud customers move to 11:11 Systems amid Broadcom shake-up
data.description:
11:11 Systems has acquired selected IBM VMware cloud customers following changes to Broadcom’s VMware Cloud Service Provider (VCSP) partner programme. The deal, announced on October 8, covers enterprise customers across North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific, and South America.

The company confirmed that the acquisition was completed, but did not disclose its financial terms. It marks 11:11 Systems’ eighth VMware-related acquisition and eleventh acquisition overall.

The transaction covers VMware-based enterprise workloads currently hosted on IBM Cloud. According to the acquisition announcement, 11:11 Systems plans to support the customers through its existing cloud infrastructure, connectivity, cybersecurity, and recovery services.

Broadcom’s VMware changes restrict cloud providers

Broadcom’s changes to VMware’s licensing arrangements began in May 2024, when cloud service providers, including IBM, stopped selling individual VMware software solutions separately. According to IBM’s official documentation, those products were incorporated into VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF), which introduced a revised pricing structure.

The changes affected customers differently depending on their licensing arrangements. IBM customers using company-provided VMware licences, or a combination of IBM licences and their own, were moved to VCF pricing. Customers using only their own licences were unaffected by that particular pricing change.

IBM also introduced revised on-demand rates and discounts for longer-term commitments. Its documentation confirms that some existing VCF for VPC customers received price reductions under the new structure.

Broadcom subsequently restructured its VMware Cloud Service Provider programme, replacing the previous arrangement with an invitation-only model on November 1, 2025. According to CRN, hundreds of former partners were excluded from the new programme, although Broadcom did not disclose the exact number.

Under Broadcom’s revised VMware partner arrangements, partners could no longer participate as both VMware resellers and cloud service providers. The company also ended its previous white-label programme. Providers that were not invited into the replacement programme could continue operating under existing contracts until their respective expiration dates, subject to the applicable terms.

The revised programme also encouraged consolidation among VMware cloud providers. Broadcom executive Ahmar Mohammad told CRN that the company wanted its remaining partners to expand through acquisitions of departing providers or their customer businesses.

Broadcom’s Infrastructure Software Group President Ram Velaga also outlined the company’s preference for providers with the operational capacity and technical expertise to support enterprise workloads. “11:11 Systems is a partner that reflects our model,” Velaga said in the acquisition announcement.

IBM was among the providers affected by the revised arrangements. On October 31, 2025, it stopped selling VMware on IBM Cloud offerings to customers who did not already have an active VMware workload on its platform.

IBM’s documentation confirms that the decision marked the end of marketing rather than the end of support for its VMware offerings. Existing customers can continue operating and expanding their environments, but they cannot purchase VMware offerings different from those they already use.

Customers using VCF as a Service also face restrictions on expanding into new regions or resource pools, switching consumption models, and adding certain backup services.

The restrictions also extend to licence portability. Under Broadcom’s VCF licensing rules, customers making new deployments after November 5, 2025, must select a certified cloud service provider to use licence portability. IBM is no longer on that list, although customers who transferred their licences before the deadline can continue using them under Broadcom’s terms.

VMware partner changes drive acquisitions

The IBM deal follows other transactions involving VMware cloud businesses affected by Broadcom’s partner restructuring. One example is 11:11 Systems’ acquisition of Digital Sense, a Brisbane-based cloud and managed services provider previously owned by Australian telecommunications company Aussie Broadband.

The companies announced the transaction in February this year. In a filing to the Australian Securities Exchange, Aussie Broadband said it had agreed to sell Digital Sense for up to A$18 million, including a conditional deferred payment of A$4 million.

The Digital Sense sale followed changes to Broadcom’s VMware partner programme and Aussie Broadband’s decision to concentrate on telecommunications under its Look-to-28 strategy, according to 11:11 Systems.

11:11 Systems had previously acquired several VMware-related businesses, including iland Cloud, Green Cloud Defense, Unitas Global, Sungard Availability Services, Faction, and Ntirety. The IBM transaction adds another group of enterprise VMware customers to its existing cloud operations.

11:11 Systems prepares customer migrations

11:11 Systems plans to migrate the acquired IBM customers to its VMware-based cloud infrastructure. The October 8 announcement states that the transaction extends its operations across North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific, and South America.

The company operates a portfolio of cloud infrastructure, connectivity, cybersecurity, and recovery services. According to its announcement, these existing services will form part of its support for the acquired IBM customers.

11:11 Systems intends to retain VMware as the underlying virtualisation platform during the transition. CEO Brett Diamond told CRN that the acquired customers would have the opportunity to move to its VMware Cloud Foundation platform without switching to a different hypervisor.

The acquisition announcement does not provide a migration timetable or customer-specific details about costs and service continuity. It also does not specify how many of the acquired customers have already agreed to migration arrangements.

The company said the transaction expands its global VMware cloud operations. Its existing infrastructure and service portfolio will support the acquired customer base as it prepares to move workloads from IBM Cloud.

data.title: Fully Managed vs. WPCO: which cloud-based Android management mode is right for your company?
data.description:
When you equip your workforce with mobile devices, you have to decide exactly how those devices will be used. For organisations using Android terminals, this choice usually comes down to two main MDM (Mobile Device Management) modes: locking the device down completely for work only, or creating a secure work container while allowing personal use.

Understanding these options is crucial. The right MDM management mode keeps your corporate data safe, while the wrong choice can lead to frustrated employees or unnecessary hardware costs.

Understanding the Corporate-Owned, Business Only (COBO) model

A Fully Managed approach, also known as Corporate-Owned, Business Only (COBO), gives IT administrators total control over the device. It is dedicated exclusively to work. Using an MDM, administrators can silently install approved business apps, block dangerous websites, disable hardware features like the camera or USB file transfer, and enforce strict password policies.

This method is perfect for regulated industries like finance or healthcare. Because users cannot install their own applications, the risk of data leaks is virtually zero. The device acts as a locked-down, dedicated business tool, keeping the corporate network completely safe from consumer apps.

The rise of Work Profile on Company-Owned (WPCO) devices

However, issuing strictly locked-down devices to corporate employees often leads to “device fatigue,” where staff must carry one phone for work and another for personal use. To solve this, Google introduced the Work Profile on Company-Owned (WPCO) enrollment method for Android 11 and above, refining an older concept known as COPE (Corporate-Owned, Personally-Enabled).

An Android WPCO configuration allows the company to retain ownership of the mobile devices while securely separating work and personal data at the OS level. Business applications, corporate emails, and internal documents are encrypted inside a dedicated, visually distinct container. The IT team manages this specific container and can enforce security policies or wipe it remotely.

Howeverthe IT department has zero visibility into the personal side of the device. They cannot monitor personal browsing history, read personal text messages, or see which consumer apps the employee has downloaded. This architecture provides the employer with hardware-level controls, such as enforcing network settings or factory reset protection, while legally and technically safeguarding the employee’s privacy on their off-hours.

Choosing the right Mobile Device Management strategy for your organisation

Selecting between these two models depends on your users. IT leaders should evaluate three main points:

  • Data isolation and compliance requirements: Fully Managed mode allows IT to enforce global device restrictions. WPCO restricts IT control to the work container and some global device settings, which is highly secure but may not meet the extreme compliance rules of certain environments.
  • Employee privacy expectations: WPCO is ideal for executives or sales teams who want the convenience of a single phone. It guarantees their privacy while maintaining corporate security.
  • Targeted attack surfaces: Fully Managed devices offer the highest security since personal apps are blocked entirely. WPCO relies on Android’s secure container to prevent personal apps (and potential malware) from accessing work data, which is safe but slightly broader in risk than a fully locked-down device.

Executing your mobile strategy
